# Guccifer 2.0 and DCLeaks: Attribution, Evidence, and Uncertainty

## Executive conclusion

The returned evidence supports an **alleged organizational attribution** of Guccifer 2.0 and DCLeaks to a Russian military-intelligence operation. The central evidence is the 2018 U.S. Department of Justice indictment, which alleges that Russia’s GRU operated Units 26165 and 74455; that those units conducted cyber operations intended to interfere with the 2016 U.S. presidential election; and that conspirators used the fictitious personas **DCLeaks** and **Guccifer 2.0** to release stolen campaign and Democratic Party materials. [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)

The indictment further alleges two particularly important persona-specific links:

- **Ivan Yermakov**, whom the indictment identifies as a Russian military officer assigned to GRU Unit 26165, allegedly participated in hacking email accounts from which campaign-related documents were later released through DCLeaks. [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)
- **GRU Unit 74455** allegedly assisted in releasing stolen documents through both the DCLeaks and Guccifer 2.0 personas. [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)

However, the returned evidence does **not** identify the individual human operator of either persona. It does not establish whether the personas were controlled by one person or multiple people, whether any named defendant personally operated either account, or whether the two personas communicated with one another.

CrowdStrike’s returned material independently documents its incident-response work for the Democratic National Committee and reports that it identified adversaries on the DNC network. It also reports that, according to cited testimony by a DNC contractor, the FBI attributed the breach to the Russian Government in September 2015. [SOURCE-2](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/) But the returned CrowdStrike excerpt does not itself provide persona-specific technical evidence or independently link Guccifer 2.0 or DCLeaks to named GRU officers.

Accordingly, the strongest source-bounded conclusion is:

> The indictment alleges that DCLeaks and Guccifer 2.0 were fictitious personas used within a GRU-linked election-interference conspiracy, and specifically alleges that Unit 74455 assisted releases through both personas. The returned evidence supports that organizational attribution as an indictment allegation, but does not establish the personas’ individual human identities or provide the underlying technical artifacts that would independently demonstrate how the personas were controlled.

## Evidentiary scope

Only two source records were returned:

1. A U.S. Department of Justice page containing the 2018 indictment of twelve Russian intelligence officers. [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)
2. A CrowdStrike account of its work responding to the DNC intrusion. [SOURCE-2](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/)

The benchmark record states that both source excerpts were truncated. The indictment excerpt had 49,838 original characters, of which 8,000 were shown; the CrowdStrike excerpt had 47,756 original characters, of which 8,000 were shown. The conclusions below therefore rely only on the returned portions.

This limitation matters because:

- The indictment’s allegations are not, in the returned record, equivalent to convictions or judicial findings after trial.
- The CrowdStrike page is a corporate incident-response account, not a criminal judgment.
- The returned evidence does not include the complete indictment, the complete technical reports, persona communications, IP records, domain records, provider disclosures, malware samples, or metadata analyses.
- Background claims from reports that were searched for but not returned cannot be treated as evidence here.

## The indictment’s alleged operational chain

### GRU units and election interference

The indictment alleges that, in or around 2016, Russia operated the Main Intelligence Directorate of the General Staff, or GRU, and that GRU Units 26165 and 74455 conducted cyber operations involving staged releases of documents stolen through computer intrusions. It characterizes those operations as large-scale efforts to interfere with the 2016 U.S. presidential election. [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)

The indictment also alleges that the twelve named defendants were GRU officers who conspired with one another and with persons known and unknown to:

- hack computers belonging to U.S. persons and entities involved in the election;
- steal documents from those systems; and
- stage releases of the stolen material to interfere with the election. [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)

These are allegations in a grand-jury indictment. The returned evidence does not establish that the named defendants were convicted or that every allegation was adjudicated.

### Targeting and theft

The indictment alleges that the operation began no later than March 2016 with compromises of email accounts belonging to volunteers and employees of Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign, including the campaign chairman. [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)

It further alleges that, by April 2016, the conspirators had compromised the networks of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and the Democratic National Committee. The alleged activity included:

- covert monitoring of dozens of employee computers;
- implantation of hundreds of files containing malicious code;
- theft of emails and other documents; and
- planning for the release of material stolen from the Clinton Campaign, DCCC, and DNC. [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)

### Use of DCLeaks and Guccifer 2.0

The indictment alleges that, beginning in or around June 2016, the conspirators staged and released tens of thousands of stolen emails and documents through fictitious online personas, including **DCLeaks** and **Guccifer 2.0**. [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)

It separately alleges that the Guccifer 2.0 persona was used to release additional stolen documents through a website maintained by an entity identified only as **Organization 1**. The alleged election-interference activity continued through approximately November 2016. [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)

This supports the following limited proposition:

- The indictment places both personas inside the alleged release phase of the same conspiracy.
- It does not, within the returned excerpt, identify the specific person or persons operating either persona.
- It does not establish that one individual operated both personas.
- It does not establish that the personas were independently controlled by separate individuals.

## Persona identities

### What the returned evidence establishes

The indictment calls DCLeaks and Guccifer 2.0 **“fictitious online personas.”** It also alleges that the conspirators used false identities and made false statements about their identities in order to conceal connections to Russia and the Russian government. [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)

The returned material therefore supports treating the personas as alleged operational identities rather than verified personal identities.

### What it does not establish

The returned evidence does not:

- name the civilian or military individual behind Guccifer 2.0;
- name the civilian or military individual behind DCLeaks;
- state that Guccifer 2.0 was personally operated by a particular named defendant;
- state that DCLeaks was personally operated by a particular named defendant;
- establish whether one operator controlled both personas;
- establish whether multiple operators controlled either persona; or
- provide account-registration, IP-address, metadata, language-analysis, or provider evidence identifying an operator.

The allegation concerning Yermakov must therefore be stated precisely. The indictment alleges that he participated in hacking at least two email accounts from which campaign-related documents were released through DCLeaks. That is a direct allegation linking him to the underlying intrusion and released material, but it is not the same as an allegation that he personally operated the DCLeaks persona. [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)

## Links to named GRU personnel and units

### Unit 26165

The indictment identifies Viktor Netyksho as the Russian military officer in command of Unit 26165 and alleges that the unit had primary responsibility for hacking the DCCC, DNC, and email accounts of people affiliated with the Clinton Campaign. [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)

It identifies other personnel assigned to Unit 26165 and alleges roles involving:

- spearphishing against campaign personnel;
- supervision of targeting activity;
- development and management of malware;
- development, customization, and monitoring of X-Agent;
- testing before deployment; and
- monitoring of malware implanted on DCCC and DNC networks. [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)

The returned indictment excerpt identifies X-Agent as a GRU hacking tool and alleges that it was used against DCCC and DNC networks. These technical allegations strengthen the alleged link between the intrusion phase and GRU personnel, but the excerpt does not directly connect each technical officer to either persona.

### Yermakov and DCLeaks

The indictment identifies Ivan Yermakov as a Russian military officer assigned to Unit 26165. It alleges that he used various online personas in hacking operations and that, in or around March 2016, he participated in hacking at least two email accounts from which campaign-related documents were released through DCLeaks. [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)

This is the most specific returned allegation connecting a named individual to the DCLeaks release path. It remains an allegation concerning participation in the compromise of accounts and the later release of material, not proof that Yermakov was the person operating the DCLeaks account.

### Unit 74455 and both personas

The indictment identifies Aleksandr Osadchuk as a Russian military officer and commanding officer of Unit 74455. It states that Unit 74455 was located at 22 Kirova Street in Khimki, Moscow, a building referred to within the GRU as the “Tower.” [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)

The returned excerpt then states that Unit 74455 assisted in the release of stolen documents through the DCLeaks and Guccifer 2.0 personas. The sentence is truncated immediately afterward. [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)

This is the strongest direct returned evidence linking both personas to a GRU unit. Because the excerpt is incomplete, no additional details about Unit 74455’s precise role should be inferred.

## Activities and distribution

The returned indictment alleges the following sequence:

1. Campaign and Democratic Party systems were targeted.
2. Email accounts and networks were compromised.
3. Documents and emails were stolen.
4. Release planning began by approximately April 2016.
5. Tens of thousands of documents were released beginning around June 2016.
6. DCLeaks and Guccifer 2.0 were used as fictitious online personas.
7. Guccifer 2.0 was also used to release material through Organization 1.
8. The activity continued through approximately November 2016. [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)

The returned evidence does not provide the individual posts, account histories, release URLs, communication records, or a complete list of documents. It therefore supports the broad alleged release function, but not a detailed reconstruction of every persona activity.

## Infrastructure and operational security

The indictment alleges that the conspirators used:

- false identities;
- false statements about their identities;
- computers located across the world, including in the United States; and
- cryptocurrency to pay for infrastructure. [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)

The returned excerpt also refers to:

- spearphishing;
- malware;
- X-Agent;
- compromised email accounts;
- DCCC and DNC network access;
- websites used to release documents; and
- Organization 1’s website. [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)

It does not include the technical artifacts needed to independently verify or reconstruct the persona infrastructure, such as:

- IP addresses;
- domain-registration records;
- hosting-provider records;
- account-recovery information;
- cryptocurrency wallet addresses;
- server logs;
- malware hashes;
- document metadata;
- email headers; or
- provider disclosures.

Consequently, the returned evidence supports an allegation of deliberate concealment and distributed infrastructure, but not a source-bounded technical attribution of either persona to a specific person.

## Incident-response evidence

### CrowdStrike’s DNC response

CrowdStrike states that the DNC contacted it on April 30, 2016 regarding a suspected breach. CrowdStrike began work on May 1, collected intelligence, analyzed the breach, and stated that it identified adversaries on the network. [SOURCE-2](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/)

It reports that a coordinated remediation event began on June 10 and lasted approximately two to three days, ending on June 13. [SOURCE-2](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/)

CrowdStrike also states that the FBI first alerted the DNC to the hack in September 2015. According to testimony by DNC IT contractor Yared Tamene Wolde-Yohannes, as quoted or summarized by CrowdStrike, the FBI attributed the breach to the Russian Government at that time. [SOURCE-2](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/)

### Limits of the incident-response evidence

The returned CrowdStrike excerpt does not disclose:

- the technical basis for identifying the adversaries;
- the adversaries’ names;
- the malware or infrastructure indicators used;
- any connection to DCLeaks;
- any connection to Guccifer 2.0;
- any connection to Unit 26165 or Unit 74455; or
- any account or infrastructure evidence identifying a persona operator.

Thus, CrowdStrike’s page corroborates that the DNC experienced a serious intrusion and that CrowdStrike performed investigative and remediation work. It also records a reported FBI attribution to the Russian Government. But, on the returned evidence alone, CrowdStrike does not independently prove the complete persona-to-GRU chain.

## Established facts, allegations, assessments, and uncertainty

### Directly established by the returned source records

The following are directly stated facts about the sources and events they report:

- The DOJ source is an indictment charging twelve named Russian intelligence officers. [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)
- The indictment names DCLeaks and Guccifer 2.0 as fictitious online personas allegedly used in the release operation. [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)
- CrowdStrike reports that it responded to and remediated the DNC intrusion in 2016. [SOURCE-2](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/)
- CrowdStrike reports that it identified adversaries on the DNC network. [SOURCE-2](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/)

### Allegations in the indictment

The following should be described as allegations, not adjudicated facts:

- GRU Units 26165 and 74455 conducted election-interference cyber operations.
- The named defendants were GRU officers involved in the conspiracy.
- The conspirators hacked Clinton Campaign, DCCC, and DNC systems.
- The conspirators stole and staged the release of documents.
- The conspirators used DCLeaks and Guccifer 2.0.
- Unit 74455 assisted releases through both personas.
- Yermakov participated in intrusions involving accounts whose contents were released through DCLeaks.
- The conspirators used false identities, distributed infrastructure, and cryptocurrency to conceal Russian connections. [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)

### Analytical assessment permitted by the returned evidence

A cautious analytical assessment is that the indictment presents a coherent alleged chain from Russian military intelligence, through GRU units and personnel, to the theft and public release of election-related materials using DCLeaks and Guccifer 2.0. The direct allegation that Unit 74455 assisted releases through both personas is especially significant because it places both personas within the alleged operational release structure. [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)

That assessment should not be expanded into an assertion that the returned record proves the personal identity of either persona operator.

### Unresolved uncertainty

The returned evidence leaves unresolved:

- who personally operated Guccifer 2.0;
- who personally operated DCLeaks;
- whether the personas shared an operator;
- whether either persona was directly controlled by a named defendant;
- what technical evidence connected Unit 74455 to the accounts;
- the complete role of Organization 1;
- the full contents of the truncated indictment paragraphs;
- the technical basis for CrowdStrike’s adversary identification;
- the existence of persona denials or alternative attribution evidence; and
- whether the indictment’s allegations resulted in convictions or other adjudicated findings.

## Resolution of competing narratives

The returned materials do not contain:

- denials by Guccifer 2.0 or DCLeaks;
- Russian government denials;
- evidence that the personas were independent activists;
- evidence that the personas were operated by unrelated individuals;
- competing forensic reports; or
- court rulings resolving the factual allegations.

Therefore, the returned evidence does not permit a balanced comparison of competing narratives beyond identifying that the indictment alleges concealment through false identities. The alternative narratives remain **unsupported in the returned record**, rather than disproven by it.

The appropriate resolution is consequently narrower than a definitive personal attribution:

- **Organizational attribution:** alleged by the indictment and directly connected in the returned excerpt to GRU Units 26165 and 74455.
- **Persona function:** alleged release channels for stolen election-related materials.
- **Individual identity:** unresolved.
- **Independent incident-response corroboration:** present for the DNC intrusion and reported Russian-government attribution, but not persona-specific in the returned CrowdStrike excerpt.
- **Adjudication:** not established by the returned materials.

## Attribution chain

The maximum attribution chain supported by the returned evidence is:

**Russia → GRU → Units 26165 and 74455 → alleged election-related intrusions and thefts → staged releases → DCLeaks and Guccifer 2.0.** [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election/)

The more specific supported links are:

- **Unit 26165 → alleged responsibility for hacking DCCC, DNC, and Clinton-affiliated accounts.** [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)
- **Yermakov → alleged participation in hacking accounts from which material was released through DCLeaks.** [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)
- **Unit 74455 → alleged assistance with releases through DCLeaks and Guccifer 2.0.** [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)
- **Guccifer 2.0 → alleged distribution through Organization 1’s website.** [SOURCE-1](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)
- **CrowdStrike → DNC intrusion response and remediation, with a reported FBI attribution to the Russian Government.** [SOURCE-2](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/)

The evidence does not justify extending that chain to a named individual as the personal operator of either persona.
